evals.prompt: Review fixtures/worker.cs for async reliability. Read-only: name every ownership, cancellation, and backpressure problem.
evals.expected_output: Names the seeded defects: unbounded Channel with no backpressure; fire-and-forget Task.Run dropping tasks with unobserved exceptions; the stopping token never threaded into Process so shutdown does not stop running work; Task.WhenAll over unbounded fan-out with no concurrency limit. Produces a lifecycle map and makes no edits.

evals.prompt: Design graceful shutdown for a worker pool: stop admitting work, signal workers, drain or discard, and await within a grace period.
evals.expected_output: Admission stop, token signaling, a stated drain/discard policy, a bounded grace period, and reporting of what did not finish.

evals.prompt: Does Task.WaitAsync(timeout, token) cancel the underlying work when it times out? What must I check before claiming the work stopped?
evals.expected_output: Explains WaitAsync throws TimeoutException but does not cancel the underlying task, and that a token not threaded into the work means the work keeps running.

evals.prompt: Our channel consumer is too slow at 40k messages/sec. Optimize the allocations and throughput and give me before/after numbers.
evals.expected_output: This is a measured throughput/allocation optimization, so it routes to the performance skill rather than async reliability.

evals.prompt: Our BackgroundService takes minutes to shut down and also pegs CPU during drain. Is that an async bug or a perf problem?
evals.expected_output: Separates the shutdown-correctness concern from the CPU cost; fixes or designs the shutdown path and defers measured CPU optimization to the performance skill.

evals.prompt: Can I use Task.WaitAsync with a TimeProvider overload in our net6.0 worker?
evals.expected_output: Gates the API on the actual TFM: WaitAsync exists in .NET 6 but the TimeProvider overload is .NET 8 or later; reports the mismatch instead of assuming.
